headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data-leakage via caveman’s MCP/file surfaces; the pair is otherwise mostly read-only on the Awesome-Prompt-Engineering side.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing repo with no runtime surfaces, but Agent B explicitly uses MCP and reads/writes files like CLAUDE.md and project notes. That creates a plausible default pathway where B ingests A-like content or shared workspace text as instructions. Because A is unverified and B’s parser behavior is undocumented, uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Agent B is connected to a shared workspace containing Agent A-generated text, THEN prompt-like content can be ingested as instructions.
IF B parses file contents from CLAUDE.md or project notes without provenance checks, THEN injected instructions can influence tool use.
mitigations: Restrict B to a read-only copy of shared text files.
Add a one-line provenance banner to any A-produced content.
Disable MCP access for the session.
Review CLAUDE.md and project notes before running B.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware parsing for file and MCP inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md, while Agent A has no declared data classes or protections. If A and B share a workspace, B can read and potentially propagate those files; B’s network egress is none, which limits exfiltration but not local leakage. The shared-file pathway is plausible in default use, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Agent A and Agent B share the same filesystem workspace, THEN B can access A-adjacent files and notes.
IF B is configured to persist session logs or memory files in that workspace, THEN sensitive local data can be copied into those artifacts.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B.
Move B’s memory/log files to a private directory.
Audit shared folders for secrets before launch.
Keep B’s network egress disabled.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B supports multiple instances and writes to files, but Agent A exposes no write, network, or concurrency capabilities at all. With A effectively non-runnable and capability-empty, there is no documented overlapping mutable resource to contend over. Any conflict would require extra orchestration not shown here, so low is the highest plausible severity.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same directory, THEN file conflicts become possible.
IF Agent B is run in multiple instances against one workspace, THEN its own writes can collide.
mitigations: Run only one B instance per workspace.
Make A outputs read-only artifacts.
Use separate output directories.
Check for stale lockfiles before starting.
requires-engineering: add workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can consume files and notes, so A-produced text can become B input if the operator copies it over or shares a workspace. A is a content-writing repository, so its outputs may be treated as authoritative prose by B unless verified. Because no verification or provenance controls are documented, the cascade is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF A-generated text is placed into B’s input files, THEN B may treat it as source material without verification.
IF B is used to draft actions from notes or CLAUDE.md, THEN errors in A can propagate downstream.
mitigations: Require a human review step between A and B.
Mark A output as draft-only.
Keep source citations alongside copied text.
Limit B to summarization, not action-taking.
requires-engineering: add provenance checks before B consumes A output.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source content-writing tools with docs-only evidence, and neither profile shows regulated data handling, residency, or certification claims. Agent B does touch session logs and memory files, but no PHI, EU PII, or retention mismatch is documented. With no concrete compliance divergence, only a low residual risk remains.
conditions: IF regulated data is manually placed into B’s memory files or session logs, THEN compliance obligations may arise.
IF future documentation assigns different residency or retention rules, THEN the assessment changes.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared notes.
Delete stale session logs after use.
Keep memory files local and minimal.
Review docs for residency/retention claims.
requires-engineering: document data-handling policy per agent.
